Grade 1 · Unit 1-A

Sound and Light

How do vibrations make sound, and how does light help us see and send messages?

Sound and light are things we notice every day, and both can be investigated with simple materials. You will see how shaking makes sound and sound makes things shake, why we only see what is lit, what different materials do to a beam of light, and how a pattern of flashes or beats can carry a message.

In this lesson

  1. Vibrations make sound; sound makes things vibrate
  2. We see only what is lit
  3. Materials in a light beam
  4. Sending messages with light or sound
  5. Try it: four stations
  6. Check yourself
  7. Play: Sound and Light

New this year: you will test how things shake, what light does, and how to send a message.

Look for the tags AnalogyDiagramTry itDataReal world

Concept 1

Vibrations make sound; sound makes things vibrate

When materials shake they make sound, and sound can shake materials.

Try it

Try it: Station 1, at the bottom of this page.

Diagram

When something shakes back and forth very quickly, we call it vibrating. Vibrating things make sound.

Hold one end of a ruler flat on a table. Flick the other end. The ruler shakes, and the shaking makes sound that reaches your ear.

“The ruler shakes. Your ear hears.”

Real world

A child hums and touches their throat.

“Feel the buzz when you hum.”

Data

Observation log, one row per test. For each test, ask: did it shake? Did it make sound?

Example log:

  • Rubber band: shake yes, sound yes
  • Drum: yes, yes
  • Humming throat: yes, yes
  • Held still: no, no

“Rubber band: shake yes. Sound yes.”

Concept 2

We see only what is lit

Objects can be seen only when light shines on them, or when they make their own light, like a lamp or the Sun.

Try it

Try it: Station 2, at the bottom of this page.

Data

Class tally, one row per object. The two answers are: seen in the dark? Seen with light?

Example tally:

  • Toy: no, yes
  • Book: no, yes
  • Lamp: yes, yes

“With light: yes. Without light: no.”

Real world

In a Michigan winter, it gets dark early. A dark bedroom is easier to see when a lamp is on.

“A lamp helps you find your toy.”

Concept 3

Materials in a light beam

Light passes through, is blocked, or bounces depending on the material. A beam is a path of light, like the light from a flashlight. Shine a beam on different materials and watch what it does.

Try it

Shine a flashlight through clear plastic, wax paper, and cardboard.

“Clear: light goes through. Cardboard: light stops.”

Data

Results, one line per material. Write what happened: through, some, blocked, or bounces.

  • Clear plastic: through / some / blocked / bounces
  • Wax paper: through / some / blocked / bounces
  • Cardboard: through / some / blocked / bounces
  • Foil: through / some / blocked / bounces

“Plastic: through. Wax paper: some. Cardboard: blocked. Foil: bounces.”

Real world

In a Michigan home, a window lets daylight in. A curtain makes the room darker, even on a sunny day.

“Window: bright. Curtain: darker.”

Concept 4

Sending messages with light or sound

A pattern of flashes or beats can carry a message across a room.

Analogy

A signal is a message sent with light or sound. A pattern is a set of flashes or beats that repeats in a rule-like way. To decode a message means to figure out what it says.

A flashlight blink is like a knock on a door. Knock or blink = the signal. The pattern of knocks or blinks = the message. The person at the door = your partner, who decodes it.

Where it breaks: a door knock is usually not a secret code, but your partner and you agree on one.

“A pattern can say something.”

Try it

Try it: Station 4, at the bottom of this page.

Data

Signal test, one line per message. Count your own.

  • Message 1: sent, decoded yes or no
  • Message 2: sent, decoded yes or no
  • Message 3: sent, decoded yes or no
  • Message 4: sent, decoded yes or no

Example: 1, 2, 3 decoded; 4 missed. 3 of 4.

“My partner got 3 of 4 messages.”

Real world

Many lighthouses flash a pattern of light that is different from the lights near them. Boats use the pattern to tell which light they are seeing. Michigan has many lighthouses on the Great Lakes.

“A lighthouse flashes to help boats.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it: four stations

Signal Device Challenge. Problem: two people need to send a message across the room without talking. Students choose light or sound, design a signal code, build a device or signal system, and test it with a partner. Criteria: the partner can decode at least one message. Constraints: use only kit materials and no spoken words.

Rotate through four stations, about 10 minutes each.

Try it

What you need

  • rubber band
  • paper cup or small container
  • plastic wrap
  • a few grains of rice
  • shoebox or small box
  • flashlight or LED lamp
  • clear plastic
  • wax paper
  • cardboard
  • foil
  • paper
  • crayons

Safety: Use ready-made flashlights or LED lamps only; do not open battery compartments or handle loose button batteries. Never shine a light into eyes. Small rice grains are not food in science class.

Try it

Station 1: Sound makers (about 10 minutes)

  1. Stretch a rubber band over an open cup. Pluck it with one finger. Does it shake and make sound?
  2. Touch the band with one finger. Does the sound stop?
  3. Cover a container with plastic wrap. Sprinkle a few grains of rice on the plastic wrap.
  4. Tap the plastic wrap gently with a pencil. Watch the rice. Does it jump?
  5. Hum and rest your fingers on your throat. Feel the buzz.
  6. Mark your log: did it shake? Did it make sound?

“Pluck the band. Watch the rice dance.”

Try it

Station 2: Mystery box (about 10 minutes)

  1. Put a small toy in the box and close the lid.
  2. Close the flashlight port. Look through the peephole. Can you see the toy? Mark no.
  3. Open the flashlight port. Look again. Can you see the toy now? Mark yes.
  4. Tell your partner what changed. The light let your eyes see the toy.

“No light: I cannot see it. Light on: I see it.”

Try it

Station 3: Light beam (about 10 minutes)

  1. Shine a flashlight on clear plastic. Write: through, some, blocked, or bounces.
  2. Do the same with wax paper, cardboard, and foil.
  3. Which material made a shadow? Which one bounced the light back?

“Clear: light goes through. Cardboard: light stops.”

Try it

Station 4: Signal device (about 10 minutes)

  1. Guess first: how many of 4 messages will your partner get?
  2. Make a code with your partner. Example: flash-flash-pause = “hello.” Tap-tap-stop = “stop.”
  3. Pick 4 messages. Send each one. Your partner watches or listens and writes what they decode.
  4. Compare. Look for: which messages got through? Were short patterns easier than long ones?
  5. Safety: Never shine a light into anyone’s eyes. Do not open the flashlight.

“My partner watches or listens.”

No time, or a material fails? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but it is better to collect your own when you can.

  • Real observation log: Students draw or mark what they observe: shaking yes/no, sound yes/no, seen yes/no, material lets light through yes/some/no, signal decoded yes/no.
  • Provided dataset: Picture cards and a simple table for backup: rubber band shaking and making sound; drum skin with rice jumping; child touching humming throat; mystery box dark vs. lit; clear plastic lets light through; wax paper lets some light through; cardboard blocks light. Use the provided dataset if materials fail or time is short.

Check yourself

What did you learn?

0 of 4 correct

Words to know

  • vibrate: shake back and forth.
  • vibration: a shaking movement.
  • sound: what we hear when materials vibrate.
  • light: brightness that helps us see.
  • material: what something is made of.
  • beam: a path of light.
  • reflect: bounce light back.
  • block: stop light from going through.
  • signal: a message sent with light or sound.
  • pattern: something that repeats in a rule-like way.
Tutor notes: misconceptions and pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Sound is a thing flying through the air.” Correct: sound is a pattern of vibrations moving through material.
  • “Sound can happen without anything shaking.” Correct: sound comes from vibrations.
  • “We can see in total darkness.” Correct: we need light to see.
  • “Our eyes shoot light to see.” Correct: we see when light enters our eyes.
  • “All materials let light pass.” Correct: some materials let light pass, some block it, and some bounce it.
  • “Light disappears forever when blocked.” Correct: blocked light does not keep going through; it may be stopped, absorbed, or reflected.
  • “A signal can work without a pattern.” Correct: a pattern helps the receiver decode the message.
  • “Signals must use words.” Correct: patterns of light or sound can carry messages.

Limits and cautions:

  • Sound making rice jump may need a loud voice, drum, or speaker; use provided data if the effect is weak.
  • The mystery box must be dark enough; test before class.
  • Flashlights need safe storage and battery checks.
  • This unit does not teach wave diagrams, sound speed, or light as electromagnetic radiation. Those belong in later grades.
  • Simplification: “light bounces into your eye” is a grade-1 version of reflection and vision.

Connections:

  • Builds on: K2.0 Science Noticing and Asking (optional), K-A Pushes and Pulls for fair-test habits, K-B Sunlight, Weather, and Staying Safe for sunlight observations.
  • Builds toward: Unit 1: Light & Matter, Unit 3: Forces, Motion & Energy, and later grades 6–8 work with waves, energy transfer, and signals.
